# Bike Wheel Build

## Overview

I built this pair of wheels over three evenings, and the third evening was mostly tension work rather than lacing. A hand-built wheel is not cheaper than a factory one, and it is not faster, but it is a wheel whose history I know, and one I can true myself when the rim takes a knock on a rough descent. The rims are shallow aluminium, the hubs are the classic cup-and-cone sort I can service with a spanner, and the spokes are plain gauge because I would rather have a wheel that survives the winter than one that saves fifty grams. When the wheels were done I rode them hard for a month and then rechecked everything, which is the step most people skip and the one that decides whether the wheel lasts. I built them because the factory wheels on the bike were heavy and had a rim I could not source a replacement for, and because I wanted to know the wheels the way I know the rest of the bike. A wheel is a simple thing made of thirty-odd identical pieces, and the only hard part is bringing them all to the same tension without losing the trueness. Everything else is patience.

## Steps

I start by laying the parts out on a cloth and putting the truing stand on the bench where I can reach both sides without walking around it. The stand holds the wheel by the axle and gives me a dial and a pointer against the rim, so I can see the movement as I turn the wheel rather than feel for it. Before a single spoke goes in I check the rim is the right one for the hub and that the spoke length matches the calculation, because discovering a length mistake after lacing is a wasted evening. I also put a drop of oil in the nipple tray so the nipples turn freely when I bring the tension up.

The lacing is three-cross with 32 spokes. I thread the first group of spokes from the hub, the ones that will lead, and I seat them in the rim in the pattern I have drawn on paper. Then I thread the trailing spokes on the same side, crossing each one over two and under one, and I follow the same pattern on the other flange. The first few spokes set the pattern and the rest follow it, so getting the first group right matters more than the last. I keep the wheel flat on the bench and check the pattern by eye before I go on.

Once the spokes are in place I bring the tension up in passes. I take every nipple a turn, then every nipple half a turn, working around the wheel rather than finishing one section at a time. Working in passes keeps the rim from going wildly out of shape and it spreads the load evenly. I oil the nipples as I go, since a dry nipple grabs the spoke and turns in jerks, which makes the tension harder to read. This part is slow and quiet, and the wheel never looks good in the middle of it; that is normal.

After the first passes I check the dish. The rim has to sit centred between the hub flanges, so I set the dishing tool across the rim and adjust the spokes on one side to bring the rim over. The dish is easy to forget while chasing the trueness, and a wheel that is true but badly dished will pull the bike to one side when it is fitted.

Then the target tension. On the drive side I aim for 120 kgf, and on the non-drive side about 100 kgf, which accounts for the shallower angle the spokes make on that side. I read the tension with a Park TM-1, taking the reading at the middle of the spoke and converting the deflection to the figure on the gauge's chart. I sample a handful of spokes around the wheel rather than trusting one reading, and I bring any low neighbours up in small steps. The tension does not have to be identical everywhere, but it should not vary by more than a small margin, because a wheel with one very loose spoke will fail at that spoke.

With the tension close I stress relieve the wheel. I squeeze pairs of parallel spokes firmly together, working around the wheel, then recheck the tension and the trueness. Stress relieving settles the spoke elbows into the hub flange and lets the wheel find its real shape, and it usually drops the tension a little, so it has to happen before the final check rather than after.

Finally the trueness. I bring the rim within 0.3 mm side to side, and I check the roundness at the same time so the wheel does not pulse under braking. I take a last pass with the stress relieving and the trueness together, going round until both hold. The last thing I do is check the spoke ends are not poking through the rim tape, then fit the tape and the tyre and put the wheel back in the stand one more time. I keep a written note of the tension readings from the drive side and the non-drive side beside the stand, so the next time I build a wheel I have a baseline to aim at rather than starting from nothing. I also record the spoke length, because a wheel that works is worth reproducing exactly, and a note is cheaper than measuring a built wheel again. The whole sequence takes about three hours once the parts are out, and most of that time is the tension passes rather than the lacing, which is why the third evening is always the longest. I do not try to rush those passes, because a wheel brought up too quickly will fight me for another hour in corrections.

## Notes

I recheck the tension and the trueness after 100 km, because a new wheel settles as the spokes bed in, and the figures drift a little in the first few rides. A quick pass with the spoke key brings them back. For spoke prep I use a drop of oil on the threads, which is enough and does not gum up like a heavy compound can. As for when to give up on a rim, my rule is simple: if a rim has taken a hard knock and will not come true without wildly uneven tension, or if it has a crack at a spoke hole, it is finished, and no amount of patience will bring it back. Rims are cheap relative to the time a bad one costs. I also keep the old rim on the wall of the shed, because a warped rim is a useful reminder of what happens when a wheel is trued by pulling a few spokes hard instead of bringing the whole wheel up together. The pair on the bike have done a full winter and a hard summer, and the tension readings have barely moved, which is the sign I was after when I built them. When I do the next pair I will lace them three-cross again, because the pattern is easy to remember and it has never given me trouble.
